The Real Reason This Problem Exists

The core issue is not regulatory—it is architectural. Payment processors like Stripe and PayPal rely on legacy banking networks that exclude West Africa by default. These systems were built for high-trust financial environments, not for regions where currency volatility and banking infrastructure are unreliable. The result is a commerce layer that fails the moment it encounters geographic or economic complexity. Digital creators in Ghana are not blocked because of policy—they are blocked because the underlying infrastructure was never designed to serve them. The solution requires bypassing these centralized systems entirely. Blockchain-based payments and decentralized infrastructure remove the need for intermediaries. This is not a patch—it is a replacement of the broken layer with architecture that works everywhere.
Why the Obvious Fixes Do Not Work

Creators often attempt workarounds like using VPNs, proxy accounts, or third-party payment aggregators. These fixes fail because they still depend on the same centralized systems. VPNs do not solve the core issue of payment network exclusion. Proxy accounts introduce counterparty risk and often violate terms of service. Third-party aggregators add another layer of dependency and fees. These are temporary hacks, not solutions. They do not address the root problem: the absence of a sovereign commerce infrastructure. A true fix must remove all centralized dependencies. It must give creators full ownership of their payment processing, file delivery, and customer data. This is what COREMERCH delivers—a complete stack where the creator owns the entire system after deployment.
